Kohath
KOH-hath
proper noun (figure / clan)
Hebrew Qohath (קְהָת) — meaning uncertain; possibly “assembly” or “allied”; second son of Levi, grandson of Jacob and Leah, progenitor of the Kohathite Levitical clan. His sons were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel (Exod 6:18), making the Kohathite line the source of both Moses and Aaron.

Biblical Definition

Kohath was the second of Levi's three sons — born between Gershon and Merari — who became the progenitor of the most sacred of the Levitical service divisions. His descendants, the Kohathites, were assigned the care and transportation of the most holy objects of the tabernacle: the ark of the covenant, the table of showbread, the golden lampstand, the altars, and the holy vessels used in sanctuary worship (Num 4:4). This was not a merely administrative role but a covenant office bounded by precise divine ordinance — the Kohathites were forbidden to touch the holy things directly; Aaron and his sons were first required to cover them, after which the Kohathites could carry them on their shoulders by their poles (Num 4:15). To violate these boundaries was death.

The theological weight of Kohath's clan resides in this elevation through restriction. That the highest objects required the most careful mediatorial covering before any mortal hand could touch them embodies the biblical theology of holiness: the holy God draws near to His people through appointed mediatorial structures, and approach on any other terms is destruction. The deaths of Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:1–2) and Uzzah (2Sam 6:6–7) stand as covenant monuments to this principle.

Among Kohath's descendants were Aaron and Moses (through his son Amram, Exod 6:20), making the Kohathite line the double source of both the Aaronic priesthood and the Mosaic prophetic office. David later reorganized Levitical service for the temple; the Kohathites retained their honorable charge (1Chr 23:12–20). The precision demanded of this clan — right objects, right persons, right procedures — foreshadows the one Mediator who would carry the holy burden of atonement on His own shoulders.

Webster 1828 Definition

Kohath: second son of Levi and grandson of Israel; progenitor of the Kohathite division of Levites charged with transporting the most holy furnishings of the tabernacle, including the ark of the covenant. Through his son Amram descended both Moses and Aaron.

KOHATH, proper noun. Second son of Levi (Gen 46:11; Exod 6:16); grandson of Jacob and Leah.

Father of Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel (Exod 6:18); grandfather of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam through Amram.

Progenitor of the Kohathite Levitical clan, charged with carrying the ark of the covenant and the most holy sanctuary vessels (Num 4:4–15); the highest and most restricted service in the tabernacle.

Key Scripture

Exod 6:16 — "And these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations; Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari: and the years of the life of Levi were an hundred thirty and seven years."

Num 3:27 — "And of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites."

Num 4:4 — "This shall be the service of the sons of Kohath in the tabernacle of the congregation, about the most holy things:"

1Chr 6:1 — "The sons of Levi; Gershon, Kohath, and Merari."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern historical-critical readings sometimes reduce the Levitical service divisions to sociological power structures rather than divinely ordained mediatorial roles; the entry recovers the biblical theology of holy-object custody.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Kohathite office has not attracted ideological revision in the contemporary sense. Certain academic approaches to the Old Testament read the Levitical service divisions as reflecting competing priestly factions in second-temple Judaism rather than divinely instituted covenant roles — treating the priestly legislation as a late composition assembled to legitimize one group's authority over another. This is rejected: the Mosaic constitution of Levitical service is the canonical datum; the antiquity and unity of the priestly narratives are presupposed throughout the canon and confirmed by their coherence with the Pentateuchal narrative as a whole. Archaeological and extra-biblical evidence neither overrules nor adjudicates Scripture on its own ground.

The deeper theological principle at stake in Kohath's story is the restriction that accompanies elevation. The Kohathites carried the most holy things — and were strictly forbidden to see or touch them under pain of death (Num 4:15, 20). This counter-intuitive severity is not arbitrary cruelty but the Bible's most concentrated lesson on divine holiness: access to the holy requires mediation, not familiarity. The modern evangelical tendency to approach God with excessive casualness — treating prayer as conversation between peers — loses the trembling reverence the Kohathite restrictions were designed to instill in Israel and, through Israel's recorded history, in the church.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew clan-name with uncertain etymology; the Kohathites are identified by their specific tabernacle assignment rather than by the meaning of their ancestor's name.

expand to see more

Hebrew Qohath (קְהָת) — second son of Levi; meaning disputed; some derive from a root suggesting “ally” or “assembly”; others leave it without certain etymology; his identity in the canon is functional, not etymological — he is defined by his descendants' charge

Hebrew bene Qohath (“sons of Kohath”) — the standard designation for the Kohathite clan in Numbers and Chronicles; the “sons” formula links them genealogically to both Levi and the covenant promise, making their service obligation covenantal in nature

Hebrew qodesh haqqodashim — holy of holies; the superlative construction meaning “the holiest of holy things”; this phrase defines what Kohath's sons were entrusted to carry, marking the Kohathite assignment as the summit of Levitical service

Hebrew massa' — burden, carrying, load; the technical term for the Kohathite and Merarite carrying-duty (Num 4:15, 24, 31); the “burden” language carries forward into the New Testament where Christ invites: “Come unto Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden” — the ultimate bearer of holy burden taking the weight from His people

Usage

"The Kohathite restriction against touching the ark — enforced by the death of Uzzah when he steadied it with his hand (2Sam 6:6–7) — demonstrates that good intentions do not override divine ordinance; the lesson Calvin draws from this incident is that human wisdom must yield to God's prescribed manner of worship, which is the root principle of the Regulative Principle."

"The reorganization of Levitical service under David (1Chr 23:12–20; 2Chr 34:12) shows that the Kohathite line retained its distinctive identity and charge across centuries of covenant history — a demonstration of God's faithfulness to the structural commitments He established at Sinai, carried forward even into the monarchy and the temple."

"The Kohathite assignment of carrying the most holy things on their shoulders by poles — never on carts, always by hand — is a type of the incarnation: the Son of God bore the weight of human sin not by remote administration but by personal embodiment, carrying the full load of atonement in His own body on the tree (1Pet 2:24)."
